title: Microbatch KV-cache Eviction and CPU/GPU Tokenizer Handoff Spec
body:
Purpose
This doc proposes an experimental design and production-ready spec for a microbatch-aware KV-cache eviction policy and a lightweight handoff protocol between CPU-based tokenization (for short/fast requests) and GPU-based batched tokenization (for long or throughput-oriented requests). Goal is to reduce end-to-end tokenization latency tail and overall tokenization CPU cost while preserving cache hit rates that benefit generation latency downstream.

Context and motivation
- Observed problem: small, latency-sensitive requests (chat turns, short prompts) frequently bypass or evict useful KV cache entries because microbatch grouping and tokenization placement are not coordinated across CPU and GPU stages. This causes scatter in generation latency and more model compute due to cache misses.
- Existing attempts (naive TTL, pure LRU) either over-retain cold prefixes or thrash under shifting workload mix (burst of demos, then steady long-form requests).
- We have two tokenizer execution modes: CPU per-request synchronous tokenizer (good for tiny requests and minimal scheduling overhead) and GPU-batched tokenizer path (used when microbatching is effective and dispatcher groups requests for kernelized tokenization). Each has different latency/cost tradeoffs and different visibility into sequence-level KV cache reuse.

Design goals
1) Minimize 95/99p tokenization latency for interactive small requests without sacrificing throughput for batched workloads.
2) Keep KV-cache effective capacity focused on hot prefixes that actually benefit generation (avoid wasting slots on ephemeral short queries).
3) Make eviction and prefetch decisions microbatch-aware: consider imminent batched workloads when evicting.
4) Keep protocol simple enough to implement in the serving runtime and compatible with our existing cache sharding and routing model.

High-level approach
- Maintain a per-shard KV-cache with adaptive scoring for entries. Score = alpha * recency_score + beta * reuse_count + gamma * microbatch_affinity. All coefficients are tunable via runtime flags.
- Microbatch affinity is a short-lived boost applied when the scheduler expects a batched tokenizer run that would reuse a prefix; affinity decays quickly (seconds) if batch does not materialize.
- Introduce a soft-reserve window: for requests marked interactive (low tokens expected), we create ephemeral cache entries on CPU path with lower base score and shorter TTL. These entries do not evict high-score entries unless shard free space < eviction_threshold.
- Implement a handoff tokenization protocol: when dispatcher decides to coalesce requests into a GPU tokenizer microbatch, it issues a \"handoff intent\" to the KV-cache on target shards with an estimated prefix fingerprint list. The cache marks those fingerprints with high microbatch_affinity for the next N seconds. If CPU path already produced entries, they can be promoted to full entries during handoff without re-encoding.

Detailed components
1) Score computation and metadata
   - recency_score: exponential decay based on last_access_ts (half-life configurable per-customer).
   - reuse_count: number of times prefix used in generation across last T minutes (sliding window). Stored as a small saturating counter (0..255).
   - microbatch_affinity: boolean -> numeric boost (e.g., +32) or small integer ramp based on predicted batch size.
   - entry_tier: ephemeral | persistent. Ephemeral entries: created by CPU path for interactive requests, TTL default 5s. Persistent: created/promoted by GPU batched path, TTL default 300s.

2) Handoff protocol (lightweight RPC between scheduler and cache)
   - API: declare_handoff(shard_id, batch_id, fingerprints[], eta_ms)
   - Semantics: cache marks fingerprints with microbatch_affinity until now+eta_ms+grace (grace 50ms). If an ephemeral entry exists, cache will promote it to persistent during this window (if promote flag present).
   - Race handling: if a GPU tokenizer arrives and a fingerprint is absent, it will still proceed; promote_on_miss is false by default to avoid stalls. Promotion is best-effort.

3) Eviction policy
   - Use a hybrid priority queue: keep top-K highest-score entries pinned; lower-score entries live in an LRU ring. When free space needed, evict from LRU ring first. If LRU ring is empty, evict lowest-score pinned entries (rare, thresholded).
   - Eviction_threshold: when free_slots < threshold, begin aggressive eviction. This threshold is per-shard and adjusted by observed per-shard request mix.
   - Microbatch-aware avoidance: entries flagged with recent microbatch_affinity are moved to the head of the LRU ring (or have a temporary score boost) to avoid immediate eviction during a batch window.

4) Cost and performance heuristics
   - CPU path creates ephemeral entries only for requests with token_count <= small_request_threshold (default 64) and where predicted generator length > 0 (to avoid caching completions-only requests).
   - GPU path uses batch_tracker to forecast next 100ms of incoming requests; if predicted batch_size >= 4, dispatcher will request handoff affinity for the top-N fingerprints observed in recent window.
   - Sampling: cache will export per-shard sampled metrics: hit_rate_by_tier (ephemeral vs persistent), promote_rate, eviction_reason histogram, and microbatch_affinity_uses.

Observability and metrics
- New metrics to add:
  - tokenizer.handoff.requests, tokenizer.handoff.successes, tokenizer.handoff.promotions
  - kvcache.entry.tier_count{ephemeral,persistent}
  - kvcache.evictions_by_reason{lru,score,capacity}
  - latency.tokenizer.cpu_p95, latency.tokenizer.gpu_p95, latency.tokenizer.end2end_p95
  - batch_prediction.accuracy (how often predicted batches materialize)
- Logging: every eviction should log sample context (shard, score, last_access_delta, eviction_reason) at debug level for 0.1% of evictions.

Experiment plan
1) Canary rollout in dev cluster: enable ephemeral entries and score compute with alpha=1, beta=2, gamma=32. Collect baseline for 48h.
2) A/B in staging: route 10% traffic to new policy with handoff intents enabled. Measure 95p tokenizer latency, generation tokens-per-second, and KV cache hit uplift. Run for 7 days across typical traffic shapes.
3) Stress test for bursty skew: synthetic workload with 90% tiny requests for 30s bursts then long tail. Confirm no catastrophic thrash.

Open questions and trade-offs
- Promotion cost: copying ephemeral entries to persistent should be as cheap as pointer flip. But implementation differs across shard store backends; need concrete benchmarks.
- Security: fingerprints may leak prompt prefixes in logs; ensure fingerprinting uses salted hashing per-tenant and never stores raw prefix text.
- Batch prediction accuracy: poor forecasts produce affinity noise and wasted memory. We need a decay constant and fallback to conservative defaults.
- Backpressure: the handoff protocol must not create backpressure loops between dispatcher and cache. Implement timeouts and best-effort semantics.

Implementation plan and milestones (rough)
- Week 0-2: implement scoring and metadata in cache shard store (no handoff path), add ephemeral entry semantics, expose metrics.
- Week 3-4: implement eviction changes (LRU ring + pinned region), add simple promote API. Run canary on dev.
- Week 5-7: dispatcher-side handoff intent emitter and GPU tokenizer adapter to consume promotions. Staging A/B.
- Week 8+: iterate on coefficients, TTLs, and fallback behaviors. Expand rollout.

Open TODOs for follow-ups
- Define serialization format for fingerprint lists (compact vector vs bloom filter). Decision depends on typical batch size; start with raw vector and revisit if RPC cost high.
- Bench: measure promotion latency for 1k promotions vs 10k promotions across shard sizes.
- Add unit tests for eviction edge cases (simulated mixed workload).

Appendix: quick glossary
- fingerprint: salted prefix hash used as KV key for cache entries.
- ephemeral entry: lightweight cache entry created by CPU tokenizer with short TTL and lower eviction priority.
- promote: operation that converts ephemeral entry to persistent (longer TTL, higher score).

If you are reading this and want to run an early experiment, ping #eng-serving-runtime with notes about your workload shape and we can reserve a dev shard for you.

Acknowledgements: Liam for batch prediction sketches, Marisol for cache metrics blueprint, Ethan for runtime instrumentation ideas.
